  s <- gsub("&", "and", as.character(arg0_s), fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("_", " ", s, fixed = TRUE)
  trimws(s)
}

fmt_yr <- function (arg0_y) {
  y <- as.numeric(arg0_y)
  if (y < 0) return(paste0(abs(round(y)), "BC"))
  if (y == 0) return("1AD")
  return(paste0(round(y), "AD"))
}

# Abstract

The Vietnamese littoral and its mountainous hinterland (318.161 km², encompassing 4.003 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells) accommodated one of the most resilient wet-rice agrarian civilisations in eastern Asia. Extending from the karst defiles and upland plateaux of the Sino-Vietnamese border across the high-energy sediment plains of the Red River Delta, along the narrow coastal corridors of Thanh Hoa, Nghe An and Thuan Hoa, across the forested Annamite Cordillera and into the vast deltaic distributaries of the lower Mekong, this terrain witnessed continuous agricultural and demographic expansion. Over more than two millennia, indigenous Austroasiatic communities transitioned from Bronze Age chiefdoms through a millennium of northern imperial administrative rule into independent dynastic monarchies that systematically expanded southward to colonise the central coast and the southern delta.

Reconstructed across five physiographic divisions from 500BC to 1862AD under MANDALA, regional population expanded from 1,05M inhabitants at the height of the Dong Son culture in 500BC to 1,45M in 1AD during initial Han provincial integration. Demographic totals rose to 1,80M in 500AD and 2,55M by 1000AD as autonomous warlord clans consolidated territorial authority following the collapse of the Tang protectorate. Following the establishment of the Ly and Tran dynasties at Thang Long, sustained reclamation of coastal mudflats, extensive dyke construction and double-cropping of wet rice propelled demographic mass to 3,90M in 1300AD and 5,10M in 1500AD under the early Le administrative reforms. Despite prolonged civil division between the Trinh lords in the north and the Nguyen lords in the south, population mounted to 6,40M in 1650AD, 7,80M in 1800AD and 10,40M at the threshold of French colonial conquest in 1862AD, yielding an aggregate regional density of 3.268,79 persons per 100 km².

The geographic distribution of demographic mass shifted markedly over this long trajectory. In 500BC, the Red River Delta accommodated 42,0% of regional population (441k people; 1.355,55 persons per 100 km²), rising to 1,07M in 1000AD and 2,14M in 1500AD, where it supported extraordinary rural densities anchored by imperial Thang Long and riverine craft villages. The North-Central plains of Thanh Hoa, Nghe An and Ha Tinh acted as a demographic reservoir and political redoubt, supporting 241k people in 500BC and expanding to 1,17M in 1500AD and 2,39M by 1862AD. Concurrently, the southern frontier in Gia Dinh and the Mekong Delta, which supported 189k inhabitants during the early historic era, expanded rapidly after 1650AD through organised soldier-settler colonies and canal excavation, surging from 1,15M in 1650AD to 1,87M in 1862AD.

This historical demographic reconstruction combines 290 catalogued settlement trajectories with systematic geoarchaeological records of deltaic progradation, archaeobotanical evidence of deepwater and double-cropped rice cultivation and dynastic archival records of registered tax households (*dinh*). By subtracting nucleated urban centres and administrative citadels from dasymetrically distributed rural cultivators, MANDALA establishes an analytical framework for long-term demographic development in Southeast Asia. The trajectory demonstrates that population expansion in Vietnam was driven by hydraulic collective engineering, communal village autonomy and state-sponsored agrarian colonisation (*don dien*).

# Background

## Fluvial Ecology and Deltaic Geomorphology

The environmental framework of northern and central Vietnam is governed by the torrential hydrologic dynamics of the Red River (*Song Hong*) and its major tributaries, the Black River (*Song Da*) and the Clear River (*Song Lo*) [@Dao2020Potential; @Taylor2001Establishing]. Rising in the Yunnan plateau of southwestern China, these river systems transport immense volumes of suspended sediment into the Gulf of Tonkin, depositing fine alluvial silts that cause rapid coastal progradation and barrier spit formation [@Dao2020Potential; @Maren2005Barrier]. The Red River Delta forms a triangular alluvial basin of 32.533 km² characterised by violent monsoon inundations, severe tidal surges, active estuarine morphodynamics and seasonal discharge fluctuations between summer monsoons and winter dry spells [@Anonymous2018Dynamics; @Lan2015Assessment].

Sedentary food production in this environment required collective human intervention to construct, reinforce and maintain continuous earthen dykes along elevated river levees [@Taylor2001Establishing; @Son2021Watersaving]. Unlike the gently overflowing floodplains of the lower Mekong basin, the Red River flows between elevated natural levees above surrounding low-lying backswamps, creating severe flood hazards during summer typhoons [@Lan2015Assessment; @Nguyen2025Risk]. Agricultural stability demanded communal water management, drainage sluices and protective polders, shaping village social structure and irrigation practices from the first millennium BC onward [@Son2021Watersaving; @Mussgnug2006Yield]. Furthermore, coastal margins remained vulnerable to marine erosion and tidal salinity intrusion, necessitating outer seawalls to protect reclaimed paddy land [@Nguyen2025Risk; @Maren2005Barrier].

South of the Red River Delta, the central coastal corridor forms a narrow littoral strip bounded by the Annamite Range (*Truong Son*) to the west and the South China Sea to the east [@Franganillo2007Bases; @Le2023Characteristics]. The north-central rivers—the Ma in Thanh Hoa, the Ca in Nghe An and the Huong in Thua Thien Hue—form isolated alluvial pockets separated by rocky headlands where spurs of the Annamite cordillera descend directly to the sea [@Le2023Characteristics]. Farther south, the vast alluvial plains of the Mekong River (*Song Cuu Long*) and Dong Nai drainage in Nam Bo present an entirely contrasting ecology, characterised by predictable annual flood pulses, dense mangrove fringes, rich freshwater fisheries and expansive tidal wetlands that supported light settlement prior to seventeenth-century reclamation [@Taylor2001Establishing; @TY2023Multiple].

## Prehistoric Foundations, Lithic Mobility, and Dong Son Statehood

Long-term human habitation in northern Vietnam extends into the Pleistocene and early Holocene, as evidenced by archaeological assemblages across limestone karst massifs and river valleys. Geochemical fingerprinting of stone tool assemblages from the Trang An Landscape Complex in Ninh Binh province demonstrates that hunter-gatherer populations maintained sophisticated mobility and exchange networks, transporting volcanic and igneous raw materials over considerable distances across lowland river margins [@Utting2022Geochemica].

The transition to sedentary agricultural society culminated in the Dong Son cultural complex (ca. 700BC to 100AD) [@Bellwood2026Year; @Anonymous2003Population]. Centred on the Red River alluvium and the Ma River valley, Dong Son communities developed sophisticated bronze metallurgy, exemplified by monumental cast bronze kettledrums decorated with feathered warriors, aquatic birds, stilt houses and ceremonial longboats [@Bellwood2026Year]. Recent nautical archaeology in the northern Red River Delta has recovered a continuous 2.200-year sequence of excavated logboats spanning from 700BC through the Han period and into the mediaeval era, confirming that waterborne mobility, riverine commerce and coastal navigation formed the technological bedrock of early Vietnamese society [@Bellwood2026Year]. Bronze socketed ploughshares, axes and harvesting sickles facilitated the clearance of lowland alluvial forests and the systematic expansion of bunded wet-rice fields [@Bellwood2026Year; @Son2021Watersaving].

Social hierarchy and defensive aggregation developed around proto-urban citadels. The massive earthworks of Co Loa Citadel, situated on the Hoang Giang river northeast of modern Hanoi, represent the foremost monument of early state formation in northern Vietnam [@Bellwood2026Year; @Franganillo2007Bases]. Comprising three concentric ramparts of tamped earth up to twelve metres high, surrounded by deep moats connected directly to river channels, Co Loa enclosed an area exceeding 500 ha and functioned as the administrative and ceremonial capital of the Au Lac polity under An Duong Vuong [@Bellwood2026Year]. Regional population during this proto-historic epoch reached 1,05M by 500BC, with demographic mass concentrated along the upper delta fans around Viet Tri and Phong Chau [@Anonymous2003Population].

## Northern Administrative Rule and Indigenous Trajectories

Following the Han conquest of Nanyue in 111BC, northern and north-central Vietnam were incorporated into the Chinese imperial administrative system as the commanderies of Jiaozhi, Jiuzhen and Rinan [@Anonymous2003Population; @Bellwood2026Year]. Chinese civil governors introduced iron-tipped ox-drawn ploughs, Chinese administrative bureaucracy and Confucian education, establishing administrative headquarters at Luy Lau on the Duong River [@Nguyen2024Religious]. Luy Lau developed into an influential international trading port and early Buddhist monastic centre where Indian and Central Asian maritime monks interacted with local elites [@Nguyen2024Religious; @Bellwood2026Year].

Imperial administration was continuously challenged by indigenous clan aristocracies. The insurrection of the Trung Sisters in 40AD united local Lac lords across sixty-five settlements against administrative taxation, demonstrating the enduring cohesion of indigenous lineage organisations [@Anonymous2003Population; @Bellwood2026Year]. Although suppressed by General Ma Yuan, who established military garrisons and colonist settlements, local lineage resistance persisted through successive uprisings, including that of Lady Trieu in Jiuzhen in 248AD [@Le2023Characteristics; @Anonymous2003Population].

During the Tang dynasty, the protectorate of Annam (*An Nam Do Ho Phu*) was governed from the fortified riverine citadel of Dai La on the site of modern Hanoi [@Hung2024Long]. Despite political subordination, the thousand-year administrative epoch transformed indigenous society, embedding Sino-Vietnamese administrative terminology and civil bureaucratic institutions while leaving communal village customs, matrilineal inheritance traditions and indigenous linguistic syntax intact [@Nguyen2024Religious; @Anonymous2003Population]. Geological resources in the north-central uplands, such as chromite and iron deposits in Thanh Hoa, supported specialised regional metallurgy and tools alongside lowland agrarian expansion [@Le2023Characteristics].

## Dynastic Consolidations: Ly, Tran and Early Le

The collapse of the Tang dynasty permitted Vietnamese military commanders to sever administrative ties with the north. Following the naval triumph of Ngo Quyen at the Battle of the Bach Dang River in 938AD—where riverine logboats and sharpened iron-tipped stakes exploited the tidal hydrodynamics of the delta—independent dynastic rule was established at the karst redoubt of Hoa Lu [@Bellwood2026Year; @Hung2024Long]. In 1010AD, Ly Cong Uan transferred the capital to Thang Long (modern Hanoi), inaugurating four centuries of centralized monarchical governance under the Ly (1009AD to 1225AD) and Tran (1225AD to 1400AD) dynasties [@Hung2024Long; @Nguyen2024Religious].

The Ly and Tran states prioritised agrarian infrastructure as the foundation of national security. Royal edicts commanded the construction of continuous river dykes (*Co Xa* dyke) to protect Thang Long from seasonal inundation, while monarchs performed annual ceremonial ploughing rituals (*tich dien*) to sanctify agricultural labour [@Hung2024Long; @Son2021Watersaving]. Concurrently, Confucian statecraft was integrated with Buddhist monastic institutions and indigenous spiritual practices, establishing an enduring tripartite ideological synthesis (*tam giao*) that legitimised monarchical authority and structured local communal administration [@Nguyen2024Religious]. State-sponsored monastic estates mobilised rural cultivators to clear coastal mangrove flats in Hai Duong and Nam Dinh, introducing salt-tolerant rice varieties and establishing double-cropping systems [@Nguyen2024Religious; @Vu2023Quality].

Under the Tran dynasty, military mobilisation systems based on soldier-farmers (*ngu binh u nong*) enabled Dai Viet to repel three Mongol invasions between 1257AD and 1288AD, preserving agricultural continuity and demographic momentum [@Hung2024Long; @Nguyen2024Religious]. Following the brief Ming occupation (1407AD to 1427AD), Le Loi established the Later Le dynasty, codified the comprehensive Hong Duc legal code, ordered nationwide cadastral surveys and implemented a systematic state examination system that established a Confucian meritocratic civil bureaucracy throughout the provinces [@Nguyen2024Religious; @Franganillo2007Bases].

## Civil Division and the Nam Tien Southern Movement

Between the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries, dynastic fragmentation divided Vietnam into competing political spheres [@Hung2024Long; @Taylor2001Establishing]. Following the usurpation of the Mac dynasty in 1527AD, the Trinh lords assumed military dominance over the northern court at Thang Long (*Dang Ngoai*), while the Nguyen lords established an autonomous principality across Thuan Hoa and Quang Nam (*Dang Trong*) [@Hung2024Long; @Franganillo2007Bases].

To sustain their independent regime against northern armies, the Nguyen lords actively promoted the southward territorial movement (*Nam Tien*) across the central coast and into the Mekong basin [@Taylor2001Establishing; @Franganillo2007Bases]. Expanding into territories previously controlled by Champa, Nguyen settlers established fortified outposts at Hue, Da Nang, Quy Nhon and Nha Trang [@Franganillo2007Bases; @Le2023Characteristics]. In 1698AD, Nguyen Huu Canh was dispatched to organise administrative districts across Gia Dinh (modern Ho Chi Minh City) and the Dong Nai plain, establishing formal Vietnamese governance over southern Indochina [@Taylor2001Establishing; @TranNguyen2018Effect].

The southern frontier absorbed thousands of landless peasant migrants from the congested northern deltas alongside Chinese Ming loyalist refugees (*Minh Huong*) who founded flourishing commercial ports at Cu Lao Pho (Bien Hoa), My Tho and Ha Tien [@TranNguyen2018Effect; @TY2023Multiple]. The state organised military-agrarian colonies (*don dien*), where soldiers and civilian pioneers drained marshlands, excavated navigable canals and converted the vast floodplains of the Mekong Delta into productive rice paddies [@Taylor2001Establishing; @Son2021Watersaving].

## Nguyen Dynastic Unification and the Eve of French Intervention

Social dislocation, onerous taxation and agrarian land alienation triggered the Tay Son peasant insurrection in 1771AD [@Anonymous2003Population; @Hung2024Long]. Led by Nguyen Hue (Emperor Quang Trung), the Tay Son overthrew both the Trinh and Nguyen lordships, expelled a Siamese expeditionary army at Rach Gam-Xoai Mut in 1785AD and crushed a massive Qing invasion at the Battle of Ngoc Hoi-Dong Da in 1789AD [@Hung2024Long].

Following Quang Trung's death, Nguyen Phuc Anh recaptured Gia Dinh, unified the country from the Chinese border to the Gulf of Thailand and proclaimed himself Emperor Gia Long at Hue in 1802AD, founding the Nguyen dynasty [@Hung2024Long; @TranNguyen2018Effect]. The Nguyen state constructed the Mandarine Road (*Thien Ly*) linking Hanoi to Saigon, erected monumental stone citadels based on Vauban designs at Hue, Hanoi and Gia Dinh and sponsored the monumental Gia Long legal code [@Hung2024Long; @TranNguyen2018Effect]. By 1862AD, when French naval forces captured Saigon and annexed the eastern provinces of Cochinchina, Vietnam had attained an all-time demographic maximum of 10,40M inhabitants [@Scornet2001Example; @Anonymous2003Population].

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Environmental Covariates

To reconstruct demographic densities across 318.161 km² of terrestrial surface, the MANDALA spatial engine partitions the Vietnamese territory into 4.003 active 5-arcminute grid cells (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km at tropical latitudes). Each terrestrial cell is evaluated against environmental covariates:
- Fluvial proximity and flood basin topology: proximity to perennial rivers (the Red, Black, Lo, Ma, Ca, Huong, Dong Nai and Mekong rivers) and active delta distributaries, accounting for irrigation water access and seasonal inundation regimes [@Dao2020Potential; @Taylor2001Establishing].
- Deltaic alluvium and geomasking: binary and continuous weights distinguishing fertile Holocene silts from acidic sulphate soils in the Plain of Reeds (*Dong Thap Muoi*) and Long Xuyen Quadrangle [@Maren2005Barrier; @Mussgnug2006Yield].
- Topographic slope and elevation penalties: penalising steep gradients across the Hoang Lien Son, Truong Son cordillera and karst plateaux of Ha Giang and Bat Dai Son while favouring alluvial plains, coastal dunes and low river terraces [@Utting2022Geochemica; @Le2023Characteristics].
- Bioclimatic suitability indices: incorporating historical rainfall data, tropical cyclone tracks, drought vulnerability indices and multi-cropping potential across humid subtropical northern zones and tropical monsoonal southern plains [@Lan2015Assessment; @Anonymous2021Assessment; @Son2021Watersaving].

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation

To eliminate double counting between nucleated urban centres and rural agricultural populations, 290 catalogued settlements with chronological population series are directly anchored to their WGS84 geographic coordinates. At each benchmark year, the active population of catalogued settlements inside each sub-region is summed and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope [@Franganillo2007Bases].

The remaining rural population is then allocated across non-settled pixels in proportion to environmental suitability weights. A two-pass boundary feathering algorithm smoothes density transitions across sub-regional frontiers, preventing step discontinuities along mountain divides and administrative limits.

## Sub-Regional Boundaries and Demographic Bounds

Every sub-regional and macro-regional benchmark estimate carries an explicit symmetric uncertainty bound (+/- 8% across all benchmark years from 500BC to 1862AD). In 1862AD, the regional total of 10,40M is bounded between 9,57M and 11,23M inhabitants. This uncertainty interval accommodates variations across historical dynastic tax registers (*so dinh*), village land cadastres (*dia ba*) and retrospective demographic evaluations [@Anonymous2003Population; @Scornet2001Example; @Franganillo2007Bases].

Table \ref{tab:subregions} documents the five physiographic divisions, land areas, benchmark populations and 1862AD densities.

```{r tbl-subregions, results='asis'}
sub_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (rk) {
  r <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  a <- as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  p_500bc <- as.numeric(r$population[["-500"]])
  p_1ad <- as.numeric(r$population[["0"]])
  p_500ad <- as.numeric(r$population[["500"]])
  p_1000ad <- as.numeric(r$population[["1000"]])
  p_1300ad <- as.numeric(r$population[["1300"]])
  p_1500ad <- as.numeric(r$population[["1500"]])
  p_1650ad <- as.numeric(r$population[["1650"]])
  p_1800ad <- as.numeric(r$population[["1800"]])
  p_1862ad <- as.numeric(r$population[["1862"]])
  dens_1862 <- p_1862ad / a * 100
  data.frame(
    Region = if (!is.null(reg_short[[rk]])) reg_short[[rk]] else clean_text(r$name),
    Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(a, 0L), " (", viscount_fmt_number(a / tot_area * 100, 1L), "%)"),
    P500BC = viscount_fmt_pop(p_500bc),
    P1AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1ad),
    P1000AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1000ad),
    P1300AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1300ad),
    P1500AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1500ad),
    P1800AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1800ad),
    P1862AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1862ad),
    Density1862 = viscount_fmt_number(dens_1862, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sub <- do.call(rbind, sub_rows)
df_tot <- data.frame(
  Region = "Regional Total",
  Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(tot_area, 0L), " (100%)"),
  P500BC = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["-500"]]),
  P1AD = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["0"]]),
  P1000AD = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1000"]]),
  P1300AD = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1300"]]),
  P1500AD = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1500"]]),
  P1800AD = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1800"]]),
  P1862AD = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1862),
  Density1862 = viscount_fmt_number(tot_1862 / tot_area * 100, 2L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_sub <- rbind(df_sub, df_tot)
viscount_table(
  df_sub,
  "Sub-regional land area, benchmark populations and 1862AD peak density across Vietnam.",
  c("Sub-Region", "Area km² (Share)", "500BC", "1AD", "1000AD", "1300AD", "1500AD", "1800AD", "1862AD", "1862AD Density"),
  list(label = "tab:subregions", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Testing and Validation

## Archaeobotanical, Nautical, and Hydraulic Verification

Sediment cores and archaeological excavations across the Red River Delta document the continuous intensification of wet-rice cultivation and hydrological modification [@Dao2020Potential; @Maren2005Barrier; @Anonymous2018Dynamics]. Pollen, phytolith and sediment analyses from late Bronze Age and early historic strata at Co Loa, Dong Son and Luy Lau demonstrate a shift from flood-tolerant floating rice varieties to short-season, higher-yielding domestic cultivars requiring bunded paddies and controlled water depths [@Vu2023Quality; @Son2021Watersaving; @Mussgnug2006Yield].

Nautical and riverine archaeological discoveries corroborate this long-term environmental adaptation. The recovery of a continuous 2.200-year sequence of excavated logboats in the northern Red River Delta, spanning from 700BC to 1500AD, provides concrete material proof of persistent waterborne transport, logboat manufacturing techniques and riverine connectivity throughout the Bronze Age, the northern administrative period and the mediaeval Dai Viet kingdom [@Bellwood2026Year]. In karst uplands, geochemical analyses of lithic tools confirm enduring raw material transport across riverine networks from early prehistory [@Utting2022Geochemica].

Dynastic chronicles record major state initiatives in hydraulic engineering. The construction of the *Dinh Nhi* dyke system in 1248AD under the Tran dynasty created continuous embankments from mountain debouchments to the sea, preventing monsoon floodwaters from submerging the low-lying rice bowls of Nam Dinh and Thai Binh [@Hung2024Long; @Son2021Watersaving]. Concurrently, coastal reclamation dykes (*de quai vac*) shielded reclaimed salt marshes from marine tidal surges and coastal erosion, allowing the conversion of brackish estuarine tracts into double-cropped paddy fields [@Nguyen2025Risk; @Maren2005Barrier; @Anonymous2021Assessment].

## Epigraphic, Dynastic and Demographic Records

Demographic benchmarks across the historical era are constrained by dynastic household registers and tax records preserved in imperial compilations such as the *Dai Viet Su Ky Toan Thu*, the *Kham Dinh Viet Su Thong Giam Cuong Muc* and the *Lich Trieu Hien Chuong Loai Chi* by Phan Huy Chu [@Hung2024Long; @Nguyen2024Religious].

Under the Han dynasty, the census of 2AD recorded 143.643 households and 746.610 registered individuals for the commanderies of Jiaozhi, Jiuzhen and Rinan [@Anonymous2003Population; @Bellwood2026Year]. Allowing for uncounted hill tribes, female under-registration and mobile foragers in the northern karst highlands, this indicates an aggregate population of approximately 1,45M people across northern and central Vietnam [@Anonymous2003Population; @Utting2022Geochemica].

During the Later Le dynasty, census surveys conducted under King Le Thanh Tong in 1490AD recorded nationwide administrative districts, commune counts (*xa*) and adult male tax-bearers (*dinh*) [@Nguyen2024Religious; @Franganillo2007Bases]. By multiplying registered adult male taxpayers by household size multipliers (typically 4,5 to 5,5 persons per taxable male) and accounting for Buddhist clergy, soldiers and unregistered dependents, historical demographers estimate a total population of approximately 5,10M inhabitants in 1500AD [@Scornet2001Example; @Anonymous2003Population]. Under the Nguyen dynasty, the cadastral registers of Emperor Gia Long (1805AD to 1836AD) compiled land allocations across 18.000 villages, providing an accurate spatial baseline for 7,80M people in 1800AD and 10,40M in 1862AD [@Franganillo2007Bases; @Scornet2001Example; @Taylor2001Establishing].

## Cartographic Ground-Truthing and Settlement Siting

Historical cartography confirms the spatial distribution of catalogued urban settlements and administrative centres. The *Hong Duc Ban Do*, an imperial atlas compiled in 1490AD, mapped provincial headquarters, river networks, mountain passes and military garrisons across Dai Viet [@Nguyen2024Religious; @Hung2024Long]. Nineteenth-century Nguyen cartography, including the *Dai Nam Nhat Thong Chi*, provided comprehensive gazetteer entries detailing provincial citadels, commercial market towns (*cho*), river ferries and coastal anchorages [@Franganillo2007Bases; @TranNguyen2018Effect].

Archaeological excavations conducted around Thang Long, Hoa Lu, Co Loa and Hue have confirmed the monumental footprints and spatial extent of historical urban defences [@Hung2024Long; @Bellwood2026Year]. At Thang Long, excavations at the 18 Hoang Dieu archaeological site uncovered uninterrupted occupation layers spanning from the Tang-era Dai La fortress through the Ly, Tran and Le palaces to the Nguyen brick citadel, confirming over a millennium of continuous metropolitan occupation [@Hung2024Long]. In the southern metropolis of Saigon-Cholon, historical geotechnical investigations and urban excavation strata confirm the rapid transformation of marshy alluvial terraces into dense mercantile settlements from the late seventeenth century onward [@TranNguyen2018Effect].

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The MANDALA source ledger for early Vietnam was compiled through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion process designed to eliminate geographic omission biases:
- Wave 1: Programmatic ingestion of official national archaeological registers and survey gazetteers, yielding 180 settlements.
- Wave 2: Extraction of site catalogues from specialised excavation monographs, colonial gazetteers and institutional reports, incorporating 78 settlements.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill and foundation-year audits, adding 32 early Bronze Age and frontier settlements.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap sweeps across all five divisions, yielding zero unaccounted settlements and confirming asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0,0%).

In total, 317 candidate localities were audited: 290 were accepted as primary catalogued settlements and 27 were excluded (predominantly duplicate administrative aliases within modern urban agglomerations or non-habitation military outposts).

# Results

## Demographic Trajectory and Macro-Regional Growth

The demographic history of Vietnam across more than two millennia demonstrates sustained long-term expansion punctuated by dynastic reorganisations and frontier colonisation (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

```{r fig-trajectory, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig2_early_vietnam_and_dai_viet_demography.png",
  "Long-term demographic trajectory of Vietnam (500BC to 1862AD), showing benchmark population growth across five sub-regions, dynastic consolidations and the southern Nam Tien expansion.",
  "fig:trajectory"
)
```

```{r tbl-benchmarks, results='asis'}
bm_years <- c("-500", "0", "500", "1000", "1300", "1500", "1650", "1800", "1862")
bm_rows <- lapply(bm_years, function (yk) {
  tot_pop <- as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[[yk]])
  rrd <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$dv_red_river_delta$population[[yk]])
  upl <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$dv_northern_uplands$population[[yk]])
  tnt <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$dv_thanh_nghe_thuan$population[[yk]])
  hig <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$dv_central_highlands$population[[yk]])
  mek <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$dv_cochinchina_mekong$population[[yk]])
  dens <- tot_pop / tot_area * 100
  data.frame(
    Benchmark = fmt_yr(yk),
    TotalPop = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_pop),
    Density = viscount_fmt_number(dens, 2L),
    RedRiver = viscount_fmt_pop(rrd),
    NorthUplands = viscount_fmt_pop(upl),
    NorthCentral = viscount_fmt_pop(tnt),
    Highlands = viscount_fmt_pop(hig),
    Mekong = viscount_fmt_pop(mek),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_bm <- do.call(rbind, bm_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_bm,
  "Benchmark population totals and sub-regional distribution across Vietnam (500BC to 1862AD).",
  c("Benchmark", "Regional Pop", "Density", "Red River", "North Uplands", "North-Central", "Highlands", "Mekong"),
  list(label = "tab:benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Six Historical Demographic Epochs

### Proto-Historic Metal Age and Dong Son Climax (500BC to 1AD)

During the middle of the first millennium BC, the expansion of bronze and early iron metallurgy across northern Vietnam supported sedentary farming hamlets along river levees. Regional population expanded from 1,05M in 500BC to 1,45M by 1AD (yielding an aggregate density of 455,74 persons per 100 km²). Settlement clustered heavily in the Red River Delta (441k in 500BC, rising to 609k in 1AD) and the North-Central valleys of the Ma and Ca rivers (241k in 500BC, rising to 333k in 1AD) [@Bellwood2026Year; @Anonymous2003Population].

The monumental fortifications at Co Loa concentrated thousands of soldiers, metalworkers and administrators, while agrarian villages cultivated wet rice using tidal irrigation and river overflow [@Bellwood2026Year; @Son2021Watersaving]. In the northern highlands, Austroasiatic and Tai-Kadai groups practised rotational swidden cultivation and terrace farming, maintaining exchange networks that supplied copper, tin and lead to lowland foundries, as reflected in lithic raw material distribution [@Utting2022Geochemica; @Anonymous2003Population].

### Northern Administrative Dominance and Local Accommodation (1AD to 500AD)

Between 1AD and 500AD, northern Vietnam was incorporated into the administrative apparatus of the Han, Eastern Wu and Jin dynasties [@Anonymous2003Population; @Bellwood2026Year]. Regional population grew moderately from 1,45M in 1AD to 1,80M by 500AD (yielding an aggregate density of 565,75 persons per 100 km²).

This period witnessed significant technological transfer, including the introduction of draught oxen, iron ploughshares, hydraulic water wheels and Chinese ceramic kilns [@Nguyen2024Religious; @Son2021Watersaving]. Administrative towns such as Luy Lau and Long Bien emerged as flourishing urban nodes accommodating Chinese officials, merchant diasporas and Buddhist scholars [@Nguyen2024Religious; @Bellwood2026Year]. However, demographic growth was constrained by recurrent peasant insurrections, heavy imperial levies and malaria along the piedmont margins [@Anonymous2003Population; @Lan2015Assessment].

### Late Imperial Administration and Tang Jiaozhou (500AD to 1000AD)

During the Sui and Tang dynasties, the protectorate of Annam (*An Nam Do Ho Phu*) was governed from Dai La [@Hung2024Long]. Regional population mounted from 1,80M in 500AD to 2,55M by 1000AD (yielding an aggregate density of 801,48 persons per 100 km²).

Under Tang administration, road networks and postal courier stations linked northern Vietnam with southern China, stimulating maritime and riverine trade [@Bellwood2026Year; @Hung2024Long]. Buddhist pilgrims visited monasteries in the Red River Delta, while local maritime merchants exported spices, kingfisher feathers, ivory and aromatic woods to Guangzhou [@Nguyen2024Religious; @Bellwood2026Year]. As Tang central authority fractured during the ninth century, local military magnates (*khuc*, *duong*) established autonomous control, constructing fortified redoubts that provided security for expanding farming populations [@Hung2024Long; @Anonymous2003Population].

### Classical Monarchies and Agrarian Intensification (1000AD to 1500AD)

The establishment of independent monarchical rule under the Ly, Tran and Early Le dynasties inaugurated an era of unprecedented demographic expansion [@Hung2024Long; @Nguyen2024Religious]. Regional population doubled from 2,55M in 1000AD to 3,90M in 1300AD and reached 5,10M by 1500AD (yielding an aggregate density of 1.602,96 persons per 100 km²).

This growth of population was rooted in systematic agrarian engineering. The royal court organised nationwide corvée labour to build and maintain comprehensive river dyke networks, shielding the delta from catastrophic flooding [@Son2021Watersaving; @Lan2015Assessment]. State-sponsored land reclamation (*khai hoang*) expanded farming into coastal salt flats, where double-cropping of early-maturing Champa rice varieties transformed agricultural productivity [@Maren2005Barrier; @Vu2023Quality; @Mussgnug2006Yield].

Thang Long developed into a major metropolis accommodating over 120k residents within royal citadel enclosures, surrounded by artisan guilds (*phuong*) and river wharves along the Red River [@Hung2024Long]. In the north-central plains, the Tran and Le dynasties founded secondary citadels, including the monumental stone-built Citadel of the Ho Dynasty (*Tay Do*) in Thanh Hoa, reflecting the strategic importance of the region as a demographic reserve [@Le2023Characteristics; @Hung2024Long].

### Southern Territorial Expansion and Civil Partition (1500AD to 1800AD)

Between 1500AD and 1800AD, political fragmentation between the Trinh and Nguyen lordships coincided with the rapid southward migration known as *Nam Tien* [@Hung2024Long; @Taylor2001Establishing]. Regional population rose from 5,10M in 1500AD to 6,40M in 1650AD and 7,80M by 1800AD (yielding an aggregate density of 2.451,59 persons per 100 km²).

While population growth in the congested Red River Delta slowed due to land scarcity and civil warfare, demographic mass expanded exponentially along the central coast and in the southern Mekong Delta [@Franganillo2007Bases; @Taylor2001Establishing]. In Nam Bo, the establishment of Gia Dinh (1698AD) and the development of commercial canal networks enabled thousands of Vietnamese pioneers, alongside Chinese merchant communities and Khmer cultivators, to transform the Mekong delta into an agricultural heartland [@Taylor2001Establishing; @TranNguyen2018Effect; @TY2023Multiple]. Gia Dinh expanded into a commercial trading metropolis of nearly 100k inhabitants by 1800AD, coordinating regional rice exports to maritime Southeast Asia [@TranNguyen2018Effect].

### Nguyen Dynastic Unification and Pre-Colonial Maximum (1800AD to 1862AD)

Following the unification of the empire by Emperor Gia Long in 1802AD, Vietnam experienced rapid demographic growth under centralized monarchical administration [@Hung2024Long; @Franganillo2007Bases]. Regional population climbed from 7,80M in 1800AD to an all-time pre-colonial maximum of 10,40M in 1862AD (yielding an aggregate density of 3.268,79 persons per 100 km²).

The Nguyen court governed from the imperial city of Hue, constructing a monumental brick citadel and palace complex along the Perfume River [@Hung2024Long; @Franganillo2007Bases]. Royal administrators sponsored extensive irrigation canals in the Mekong Delta, including the monumental Vinh Te Canal linking Chaudoc to the Gulf of Thailand, which facilitated military movement and agricultural settlement [@Taylor2001Establishing; @TY2023Multiple]. By 1862AD, the Red River Delta accommodated 4,37M inhabitants (42,0% of regional population; 13.426,37 persons per 100 km²), North-Central Vietnam housed 2,39M, Cochinchina accommodated 1,87M, the Northern Uplands supported 1,14M and the Central Highlands supported 624k [@Scornet2001Example; @Anonymous2003Population].

## Urban Hierarchy and Settlement Systems

Table \ref{tab:leading_settlements} presents the leading fifteen catalogued settlements in Vietnam ordered by peak population.

```{r tbl-leading-settlements, results='asis'}
set_list <- unname(set_data)
sett_peaks <- vapply(set_list, function (s) {
  if (is.null(s$population) || length(s$population) == 0) return(0)
  max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))
}, numeric(1))

ord <- order(sett_peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_sett <- set_list[ord]

top_rows <- lapply(head(top_sett, 15), function (s) {
  p_max <- max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))
  p_1862 <- if (!is.null(s$population[["1862"]])) as.numeric(s$population[["1862"]]) else "-"
  lat <- as.numeric(s$coords[[1]])
  lon <- as.numeric(s$coords[[2]])
  coord_str <- paste0(viscount_fmt_number(abs(lat), 2L), if (lat >= 0) " N" else " S", ", ",
                      viscount_fmt_number(abs(lon), 2L), if (lon >= 0) " E" else " W")
  reg_lbl <- if (!is.null(reg_short[[s$region_id]])) reg_short[[s$region_id]] else clean_text(s$region)
  data.frame(
    Name = clean_text(s$name),
    SubRegion = reg_lbl,
    Coordinates = coord_str,
    PeakPop = viscount_fmt_pop(p_max),
    P1862AD = if (is.numeric(p_1862)) viscount_fmt_pop(p_1862) else "-",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_top <- do.call(rbind, top_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_top,
  "Leading fifteen historical settlements across Vietnam, showing coordinates, peak population and 1862AD population.",
  c("Settlement Name", "Sub-Region", "Coordinates", "Peak Pop", "1862AD Pop"),
  list(label = "tab:leading_settlements", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

The historical settlement hierarchy conformed to a multi-tiered structural organisation:
1. Primary imperial capitals and commercial metropolises (> 100k inhabitants): Thang Long (modern Hanoi, 121,05k in 1500AD, 111,42k in 1300AD), Ho Chi Minh City/Saigon-Cholon (modern metropolitan anchor, 1,11M peak; historical Gia Dinh, 95,28k in 1800AD), Hai Phong (historical estuarine trading hub, 207,92k peak) and Can Tho (Mekong regional node, 246,12k peak).
2. Major regional citadels and coastal ports (50k to 100k inhabitants): Da Nang (Tourane, 216,41k modern peak; historical maritime gateway), Phu Xuan/Hue (imperial capital of the Nguyen dynasty, 45k in 1800AD, 52k in 1862AD), Bien Hoa (Cu Lao Pho, 100,76k peak), Ben Tre (101,18k peak) and My Tho (commercial port on the Tien Giang).
3. Secondary provincial fortresses and craft centres (10k to 50k inhabitants): Citadel of the Ho Dynasty in Thanh Hoa, Hoa Lu in Ninh Binh, Luy Lau in Bac Ninh, Pho Hien in Hung Yen (international trading port of the seventeenth century) and Nam Dinh (textile and administrative centre).
4. Tertiary agrarian villages, market communes and border garrisons (< 10k inhabitants): Co Loa Citadel, Dong Son type-site, Oc Eo, Angkor Borei and hundreds of walled agrarian communes (*xa*) catalogued throughout the lowlands.

# Limitations

Historical demographic analysis across Vietnam remains subject to distinct documentary and preservation constraints:
1. Differential preservation of historical records: recurrent warfare, foreign invasions and tropical humidity led to the destruction of major imperial libraries, most notably during the Ming invasion of 1407AD when the Yongle emperor commanded the confiscation and destruction of Vietnamese books and archival records [@Hung2024Long; @Nguyen2024Religious].
2. Tax register under-enumeration: dynastic censuses (*so dinh*) recorded adult males liable for taxation, military conscription and corvée labour, systematically omitting females, infants, elderly individuals and unintegrated upland minority groups [@Scornet2001Example; @Anonymous2003Population].
3. Fluvial and marine alluviation: active sedimentation in the Red River Delta and coastal erosion along the central coast have buried early prehistoric and historic sites beneath metres of silt or submerged coastal harbour installations [@Dao2020Potential; @Maren2005Barrier; @Nguyen2025Risk].
4. Fluid frontier boundaries: the historical southward expansion (*Nam Tien*) created shifting ethnolinguistic boundaries where Vietnamese, Cham, Khmer and upland populations coexisted, complicating ethnic population attributions prior to nineteenth-century cadastral surveys [@Anonymous2003Population; @Taylor2001Establishing].

# Conclusion

Early Vietnam and Dai Viet sustained one of the most remarkable demographic expansions in pre-modern Southeast Asia, expanding from 1,05M inhabitants at the height of the Dong Son culture in 500BC to 10,40M at the threshold of French colonial intervention in 1862AD across 318.161 km² of territory. This achievement was rooted in the collective engineering of extensive dyke networks in the Red River Delta, the adoption of double-cropped wet rice and the state-sponsored agrarian colonisation of the southern frontier.

The long-term trajectory reveals that population growth was intimately linked to the institutional strength of communal villages and centralised monarchical administration. Through the combination of communal village autonomy, military-agrarian colonies (*don dien*) and meritocratic bureaucratic governance, Vietnamese society maintained civilisational cohesion while absorbing diverse ecological zones from the northern mountains to the Mekong Delta.

# Appendix

The MANDALA source ledger integrates 290 primary catalogued settlements across five sub-regions, reconciled against national heritage inventories, excavation monographs and historical gazetteers. Table \ref{tab:saturation} summarises the four-wave saturation audit demonstrating complete regional coverage.

```{r tbl-saturation, results='asis'}
sat_waves <- led_data$saturation_audit$waves
sat_rows <- lapply(sat_waves, function (w) {
  data.frame(
    Wave = paste0("Wave ", w$wave),
    SourceClass = clean_text(w$source_class),
    PriorTotal = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(w$prior_cumulative_included), 0L),
    NewlyIncluded = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(w$newly_included), 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sat <- do.call(rbind, sat_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_sat,
  "Four-wave asymptotic saturation audit of catalogued settlements across Vietnam.",
  c("Ingestion Wave", "Source Category", "Prior Cumulative", "Newly Included"),
  list(label = "tab:saturation", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```
